name: Neodata
tagline: Mexican construction software suite: unit price budgeting, insumo catalogs, and site ERP modules.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The math inside a unit price budget is not hard: explode a concepto into materials, labor and equipment, stack indirect cost, financing and profit, print the sheet. An agent will give you that in a weekend, and for your own private estimating it may genuinely be enough. What it will not give you is the maintained catalog of insumos and regional prices, the nested basic-unit libraries that took years to assemble, or the export formats that reviewers of Mexican public works tenders expect to open without argument. On top of that sits the ERP half: purchasing, warehouse, estimates against contract, payroll for site crews, all of it multi user with an audit trail. Build the calculator if you want to understand your own numbers, but if your budget has to survive a tender review, you are buying the paperwork compatibility, not the arithmetic.
coreLoopDIY: A local estimating app where you keep your own insumo catalog, build nested unit prices, apply the indirect and profit factors, and export budget plus analysis sheets to PDF and XLSX.
requirements: Your own insumo prices, typed in or imported as CSV
Someone willing to keep those prices current
Independent verification of the factor math before it goes near a signature
whatYouLose: Maintained insumo and regional price catalogs, updated for you instead of by you
Prebuilt unit price and basic-unit libraries covering thousands of common conceptos
Export and interchange formats that tender reviewers and government platforms accept without a fight
The ERP side: purchasing, warehouse, contract estimates, site payroll, all with permissions and history
Support, training and the plain fact that the person auditing your file already knows the software
moatNotes: The catalogs and the accepted file formats are the product. The calculator is the demo.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a construction budget is not really a spreadsheet, it is a document that other people have to accept. Contractors pay for a price catalog someone else keeps current, for unit price libraries they did not have to key in, and for output that lands in a reviewer's hands in a shape that reviewer has seen a thousand times. Add the years of historical budgets already living in the format, plus the ERP modules the finance team wired into their month end, and switching becomes a project rather than a decision. A personal estimator built in a weekend competes with none of that; it competes with your own notebook, which is a fair fight and sometimes the right one.
notes: The unit price arithmetic is a weekend build; the catalog and the paperwork are not. The moat is maintained insumo pricing plus export formats that Mexican public works reviewers already trust.
prompt:
Build a local unit price estimating tool for construction budgets. Single user, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, not a menu: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLite through the stdlib sqlite3 module, Jinja2 templates with HTMX for interactivity, ReportLab for PDF, openpyxl for XLSX. One repo, started with: uvicorn app.main:app --reload. Database lives at ./data/estimates.db.

Data model:
- insumo: code, description, unit, unit_cost, kind (material, labor, equipment, tool)
- concepto: code, description, unit, plus component rows referencing either an insumo or another concepto, each with a quantity
- presupuesto: name, client, plus rows referencing a concepto with a quantity
- factor set per presupuesto: indirect cost pct, financing pct, profit pct, additional charges pct

In scope:
1. CSV import and export for insumos and conceptos so catalogs stay portable.
2. Recursive cost explosion where a concepto can nest other conceptos as basic units. Detect cycles and fail loudly with the offending path.
3. Recalculate an entire budget when any insumo price changes, and show the delta against the last saved snapshot.
4. Snapshots: freeze a budget with the prices used, then diff two snapshots line by line.
5. Exports: budget summary, one unit price analysis sheet per concepto, and total insumo explosion, as both PDF and XLSX.
6. Escalation tool: bump every insumo of one kind by a percentage, preview the effect on the budget total, then commit or discard.

Out of scope, do not build: purchasing, warehouse, payroll, scheduling, multi user permissions, any government tender interchange format, any bundled price catalog. Ship an empty catalog plus a seed script with ten fake insumos for testing.

Write pytest tests for the explosion math, the cycle detector, and the factor stack applied in the correct order.

No API keys are needed. If anything becomes configurable, read it from .env and commit a .env.example only.

README: how to run it, how to import a CSV catalog, and a blunt warning that the arithmetic is the user's to verify before anyone signs a contract based on it.
